summary:
Main recommendation: compute the heart vector with an equivalent double layer (EDL, the ECGSIM-style source) collapsed into one dipole per surface face, instead of hand-placing wavefront dipoles. Each mesh face or patch p (endocardial or epicardial side of a region) has area A_p, centroid x_p, unit normal n_p pointing out of the myocardium, and a normalized membrane-potential template s_p(t) between 0 and 1. The face dipole is m_p(t) = -tau*A_p*n_p*s_p(t), with tau = 0.2 S/m x 40 mV = 8 mA/m. The heart vector is H(t) = sum of m_p. This follows from J_i = -sigma*grad(Vm) and the gradient theorem, and is the same as the EDL of van Oosterom, ECGSIM and Boonstra 2022.

What this one formula gives for free:
(a) The QRS comes from the order of the upstrokes.
(b) If the surface is closed (sum of A_p*n_p = 0), the baseline and ST segment are flat when every face is on its plateau.
(c) The T wave comes only from differences in repolarization time. The vector points toward the faces that repolarize first.
(d) The ventricular gradient G = integral of H dt = -tau * sum(A_p*n_p*APD_p). It does not depend on the activation order, which matches Wilson and Burger. So if the APD map is tied to anatomy, bundle branch block, PVC and paced beats get discordant ('secondary') ST-T without any extra rule.
(e) Ischemia: lowering the plateau or raising the resting level of ischemic faces gives an ST vector along those faces' normals. It points outward (ST elevation) for epicardial or transmural injury and into the cavity (ST depression) for subendocardial injury. This agrees with the Aidu/Titomir boundary double layer and with clinical ST rules.
(f) Old MI: set a dead region's s to 0 and close the surface with rim faces. The vector that region would have produced disappears, so Q waves appear. This is the Selvester principle.

Timing data to use:
- Endocardial LV breakthrough in three areas at 0-5 ms, merged by 15-20 ms. RV starts 5-10 ms after the LV (Durrer 1970).
- First RV epicardial breakthrough within 25 ms of QRS onset; LV breakthroughs about 7 ms later; all breakthroughs by 40 ms; last to activate is the basal LV and/or the RV outflow tract (Ramanathan 2006).
- Spread along the wall 0.85 m/s and 2.5x slower across the wall (Boonstra).
- Mean ARI (a proxy for local APD) 235 ms; LV apex-to-base spread 42 ms (range 30-52); LV ARI longer than RV by 32 ms (Ramanathan).
- Best-fitting gradient in EDL T-wave fits: apex-to-base 65 ms (transmural 30 ms or interventricular -8 ms when used alone) (Kloosterman 2023).
- Endocardium-to-epicardium APD difference 25 ms in the LV and 20 ms in the RV (Szathmary 2005).
- MAP duration falls 1.44 ms per ms of later activation (Cowan 1988).

Converting H(t) to leads: an infinite homogeneous medium will not give realistic chest-lead R progression. Use the Dower rows as fixed lead vectors on H(t), after mapping your app axes to Frank axes (X left, Y down, Z back; this convention is my inference and must be checked). Fallback and calibration target: the FECGSYN 'normal' Gaussian VCG built on Sameni's model. When I pushed it through Dower I got a frontal QRS axis of +17 deg, transition at V2-V3, concordant T and a spatial QRS-T angle of 48 deg. Normal targets: SVG 79-107 mV·ms, P under 120 ms and under 0.25 mV, QRS under 110-120 ms.

Caution: a naive activation model (6 foci at 0.85 m/s) gave clinically abnormal QRS patterns. Expect to tune each focus's timing. If tuning fails, fit non-negative weights for each region's contribution to a target VCG (NNLS) so every lead is still a projection of the same H(t).

findings.topic: 1. Simplified forward models: EDL/UDL (ECGSIM), multi-dipole, and what each published model specifies
findings.detail: ECGSIM (van Oosterom & Oostendorp 2004): EDL on the closed surface around the ventricular myocardium. 257 nodes from MRI; transfer matrix to 198 thorax sites; Phi = A*S (A is LxN, S is NxT). Each node's source strength follows a TMP template set by depolarization time delta_n and repolarization time rho_n, with local APD alpha_n = rho_n - delta_n and an upstroke scale m_n (default 100%). Realistic torso with lungs and blood cavities. Wider spread of repolarization times gives larger T waves. Boonstra 2022 (Frontiers): Phi(t,y) = integral over Sv of A(y,x)*Vm(t,x) d(omega)(y,x), where omega is the solid angle. Strength is calibrated to a 40 mV step across the activation wavefront in tissue of 0.2 S/m, i.e. 8 mA/m. The paper prints '8 A/mm', which is a typo: its own 50% value is written as 4 mA/m. A scar or diseased patch breaks the EDL equivalence unless the new boundary is added. Old MI was earlier modelled by cutting a hole in the anatomy (Oostendorp & Ham 2001). Boonstra's activation used a fastest-route algorithm at 0.85 m/s along the surface, 2.5x slower across the wall (about 0.34 m/s), with 6 starting sites. Their patient-specific case used 8 foci at 1 m/s and gave QRS 100 ms. Szathmary 2005: 1 mm^3 elements, 142,200 in total. The wall was cut into 5 layers. Transmural MAP-duration gradient 25 ms in the LV and 20 ms in the RV. Torso relative conductivities: cavities 3.5, lungs 0.25. The single-dipole heart vector matched the Frank-measured VCG vector with r = 0.957-0.991 and R^2 = 91-99%, but deviated by up to 28.5% of the peak VCG during the middle third of the QRS (mostly in z and y). Kloosterman 2023 conductivities as printed: myocardium 0.2, blood 0.6, thorax 0.4, lungs 0.2 S/m (the thorax value is unusual). Miller & Geselowitz 1978 (Circ Res 43:301-315) linked cellular action potentials to the body-surface ECG for normal and abnormal hearts; I could not retrieve its region and dipole tables. Lorange & Gulrajani 1993 (J Electrocardiol 26:245-261 and 263-277) is an anisotropic-propagation ventricular model of normal activation and conduction block; tables not retrieved. Rueda et al. 2022 (arXiv 2202.03938) is a 5-dipole parametric model with one dipole per P, Q, R, S and T wave; it is an alternative fallback.

findings.topic: 2. Core physics: from membrane potential to H(t), with sign, closure and ventricular-gradient properties
findings.detail: Dipole in an infinite homogeneous conductor (bem.fi Eq. 8.12/8.15): Phi = (1/(4*pi*sigma)) * p·(r - r0)/|r - r0|^3 = p*cos(theta)/(4*pi*sigma*r^2), with p in A·m and sigma in S/m. Impressed current: J_i is proportional to -grad(Vm) (bem.fi Eq. 8.34-8.35). Double-layer field (Eq. 8.28): the integral of strength times (n·grad)(1/r) over the surface. Derivation (mine; marked unsourced): H = integral of J_i dV = -sigma * integral of grad(Vm) dV = -sigma * closed-surface integral of Vm*n dS. Discretized: H(t) = -tau * sum_p A_p*n_p*s_p(t), with tau = 8 mA/m and n_p pointing out of the myocardium (into the cavity on endocardial faces). Sign check: when the endocardium is depolarized and the epicardium is at rest, H = -tau*A*n_endo, which points from cavity to epicardium, the direction of travel. Closed surface (sum of A_p*n_p = 0): H = 0 when every face is at rest or on its plateau, so baseline and ST are isoelectric. If the template area equals APD, G = integral of H dt = -tau * sum(A_p*n_p*APD_p). That depends only on the APD map, which is Burger's 1957 theorem that the ventricular gradient does not depend on activation order. G points toward the shortest-APD regions, as Waks states. Example size (derived): a 20 cm^2 patch has m = 8e-3 A/m * 2e-3 m^2 = 1.6e-5 A·m. Along its axis at 10 cm in 0.2 S/m that gives 1.6e-5/(4*pi*0.2*0.01) = 0.64 mV, before any torso boundary gain.

findings.topic: Normal ventricular activation timing and conduction velocities (inputs for the conduction graph)
findings.detail: Durrer 1970 (7 isolated human hearts, up to 870 intramural terminals): three LV endocardial areas fire 0-5 ms after LV onset. They are the anterior and posterior paraseptal wall and the central left septal surface. They grow quickly over 5-10 ms and merge by 15-20 ms. The septum starts in its middle third on the left side. The RV starts near the anterior papillary muscle insertion 5-10 ms after LV onset. The last areas are the posterobasal LV and the pulmonary conus. Ramanathan 2006 (noninvasive imaging, 7 healthy adults aged 21-43): the first epicardial breakthrough is RV anterior-paraseptal, within 25 ms of QRS onset. Posterior LV electrograms show q waves of about 30 ms from left-to-right septal activation. LV breakthroughs (anterior-paraseptal) come on average 7 ms after the RV breakthrough. All breakthroughs occur within 40 ms. The posterior LV activates apex to base, and the last region is the posterior or posterolateral basal LV and/or the RV outflow tract. The anterior RV shows an rS with r about 0.7 mV. Atrial conduction is 80-100 cm/s, ending at the LA appendage. CVPhysiology: SA node to atrial muscle about 0.5 m/s; AV node about 0.05 m/s; His bundle and bundle branches about 2 m/s; Purkinje about 4 m/s; atria activated within about 90 ms. Ventricular muscle 0.85 m/s along the surface, 2.5x slower across the wall (Boonstra).

findings.topic: 3. Repolarization parameters for the T wave (gradients, TMP template, APD-AT coupling)
findings.detail: Ramanathan 2006: mean epicardial ARI (proxy for APD) 235 ms. Subject 1: 256 ms (191-329). LV apex-to-base ARI spread averages 42 ms (30-52). LV ARI exceeds RV by 32 ms. In normal hearts the repolarization order is set by local APD, not by activation order, because activation differences are much smaller than APD differences. Under ectopy or pacing the activation differences become larger than the APD differences, so the repolarization order follows activation. Kloosterman 2023 (EDL with 67-lead maps, 9 controls): TMP template Vm(t) = (1 - a*t) * 1/(1 + exp(R*(t - Trep))). 'a' is a linear plateau decline of 5/10/20/40% at 200 ms; t is time after depolarization ends; Trep is local repolarization time; R comes from the dominant T wave. Amplitude 40 mV. T was concordant when epicardial RT was shorter than endocardial RT, when RT increased from apex to base, or when LV RT was shorter than RV RT. Best fit was apex-to-base alone at 65 ms (56-67) (r = 0.83, RD 0.67). Transmural alone was 30 ms (r = 0.77, RD about 2.0). Interventricular alone was -8 ms (r = 0.72). The combined fit (apex-to-base base plus transmural 0 to 2 ms and interventricular -1 to -3 ms) improved RD to 0.59. Opthof 2017 (3 donor hearts): gradients in all axes; no late repolarization in the mid-wall; activation and repolarization are inversely related along the epicardium but positively related over the whole heart. Cowan 1988 (MAP at 8-10 LV epicardial sites, 15 patients): with upright T, MAP duration falls with later activation (mean slope -1.44), and repolarization spread (14 ms) is smaller than activation spread (23 ms). With T inversion from aortic stenosis there is no relation, and repolarization spread is 31 ms versus activation 26 ms. Franz 1987 (Circulation 75:379) reported the same inverse APD-AT relation. Szathmary: endocardium minus epicardium APD 25 ms in the LV and 20 ms in the RV.

findings.topic: Ventricular gradient (Wilson) and normal QRS-T relations: targets for primary vs secondary T
findings.detail: Waks & Tereshchenko 2016 (J Electrocardiol 49:824): SVG = [integral of Vx, integral of Vy, integral of Vz] over QRS onset to T end, i.e. the QRS area vector plus the T area vector. It points from the region with the longest mean duration of the excited state toward the region with the shortest. Burger 1957 showed it does not depend on activation order; Geselowitz showed it depends on action-potential area, shape and duration. A_T = -A_QRS + G: purely secondary changes leave G unchanged, while primary changes (e.g. ischemia) change it. Normal values in 660 healthy people: SVG magnitude median 107 mV·ms in men (59-187) and 79 mV·ms in women (39-143). Azimuth -24 deg (men, -52 to 13) and -15 deg (women, -38 to 20). Elevation about 29 deg (8-48). A larger population gave 60.4 vs 52.5 mV·ms. Unit test for our model: changing the activation order (e.g. LBBB) with a fixed APD map should leave G almost unchanged.

findings.topic: Selvester QRS score / old MI simulation
findings.detail: Origin: the score was first developed from computer models of the heart's activity and validated against post-mortem specimens. Original version: 54 criteria, 32 points, each about 3% of LV mass. Simplified version: 37 criteria, 29 points (Bounous 1988). Updated version: 50 criteria, 31 points, including QRS fragmentation and 'confounders' (LBBB, LVH, etc.). Leads used: I, II, aVL, aVF and V1-V6. Measurements: Q and R durations, R and S amplitudes, R/Q and R/S ratios. Infarcts localized to 12 LV segments (Selvester, ISCE 1982). The LBBB variant maps to 5 segments: septal, anterior (formerly anteroseptal), lateral (formerly anterosuperior/posterolateral), plus inferior and posterior. Modelling principle: removing an infarcted segment's depolarization vector during its normal activation window turns the early QRS vector away from the infarct, giving Q waves or reduced R in leads facing it.

findings.topic: 5. Current of injury: direction, magnitude, systolic vs diastolic, and adding it as a 3D term
findings.detail: Aidu et al. 2003 (Titomir/Szathmary): an acute ischemic zone acts as a uniform double layer on the ischemic-healthy boundary. Its moment density is proportional to the difference in action-potential amplitude and points from healthy toward ischemic tissue. It is largest with complete injury. The total ST heart vector is proportional to that difference times the area of the boundary projected onto the plane perpendicular to the vector. It points along the wall normal near the middle of the ischemic zone. ST shift is assessed in mid-ST. Transmural or subepicardial injury points the ST vector endocardium-to-epicardium, giving ST elevation in facing leads and reciprocal depression opposite. Subendocardial injury points it epicardium-to-endocardium (toward the cavity), giving ST depression that localizes poorly. Hyperacute T waves appear within seconds and fade within minutes (ECGwaves). Systolic injury current points toward the injured region (ST shift); diastolic current points toward healthy tissue (TQ depression, which shows as further ST elevation once the baseline is set to TQ). Bidomain ischemia models use a 30 mV ischemic-vs-healthy membrane-potential difference during ST and a border zone of about 3 mm. Canine needle data: ischemic isosurface at 11 mV, peak 18-26 mV. Clinical thresholds (4th Universal Definition of MI): new J-point ST elevation in 2 contiguous leads of at least 1 mm (0.1 mV), except V2-V3: at least 2 mm in men 40 or older, 2.5 mm in men under 40, 1.5 mm in women. ST depression of at least 0.5 mm in V1-V3 with positive T suggests posterior STEMI. In the EDL model (derived): reduce plateau by eps_p, giving H_ST = +tau * sum over ischemic faces of eps_p*A_p*n_p. Raise rest level by r_p, giving H_TQ = -tau * sum of r_p*A_p*n_p. These reproduce the epicardial and subendocardial rules automatically.

findings.topic: 4a. Atrial dipole: P wave, RA/LA components, P-mitrale/P-pulmonale, Ta wave
findings.detail: LITFL: normal P under 120 ms, under 0.25 mV in limb leads, under 0.15 mV in chest leads; axis 0 to +75 deg. The RA forms the first third of the P wave, the LA the last third, and both overlap in the middle third. V1 P is normally biphasic with roughly equal parts. P-mitrale (LA enlargement): duration over 120 ms, notch near the peak, terminal negative V1 component over 40 ms wide and over 1 mm deep. P-pulmonale (RA enlargement): P in II over 2.5 mm; initial positive P in V1 over 1.5 mm. Ramanathan: atrial activation spreads from the SA node and ends at the LA appendage, at 80-100 cm/s. Ta wave (Holmqvist 2009, 40 patients in complete AV block): opposite polarity to P and 2-3x its duration; Ta duration 323 +/- 56 ms against P 124 +/- 16 ms. Frank-lead Ta peaks: Y -6.9 +/- 3.9 µV at 196 ms, X -4.1 µV at 216 ms, Z -1.7 µV at 335 ms. Another study: largest Ta in II (-25 +/- 16 µV), V2 (-22), V3 (-21), V4 (-20). Ta can last more than 400 ms after P, so it can shift the ST segment, especially in tachycardia or short PR. Guillem 2006: the P-loop is better recovered with a P-specific matrix than with Dower (12.2 vs 14.4 µV RMS error), because the atrial source sits at a different place than the ventricles.

findings.topic: 4b. Atrial flutter and AF source models
findings.detail: Typical flutter: counterclockwise macroreentry around the tricuspid annulus through the cavotricuspid isthmus (about 90% of cases). Atrial rate 240-350/min. Negative sawtooth waves in II, III and aVF with positive waves in V1. The wave has a slow downslope followed by a sharp negative deflection. Clockwise flutter gives broad positive inferior waves. Vector sequence for counterclockwise flutter (Ng/Sahakian CinC 2004): isoelectric, then trough in II, peak in V1, peak in II, trough in V1. So the inferior and anterior components are about 90 deg out of phase, which is a rotating vector. Narayan CinC 2003: isthmus-dependent flutter loops are coherent in all 3 planes (19/19), non-isthmus flutter in up to 1 plane, and AF in none (irregular, space-filling). AF f-wave model (Stridh & Sörnmo sawtooth, generalized by Malik 2017): amplitude a1(t) = a0 + Delta_a*sin(random walk); frequency f1(t) = f0 + Delta_f*sin(random walk); f(t) = sum over m = 1..M of weighted a1(t)*sin(2*pi*m*integral of f1). Parameters: M = 3; a0 = 0.06 +/- 0.02 mV; Delta_a = a0/2; f0 = 6 +/- 2 Hz; Delta_f = f0/3; random-walk steps 0.02 and 0.1; plus 2-7 Hz band-passed noise at 50 +/- 20%; polarity flipped at random; 15 Hz low-pass. Stridh 2002: faster AF tends to look sinusoidal, slower AF sawtooth-like. Median f-wave amplitude in V1 is 46 µV (Sci Rep 2019). A dominant V1 rate of 390/min or more points to long-standing persistent AF.

findings.topic: 6. Sameni 3D dynamic VCG model: equations and a normal parameter set (FECGSYN case 1)
findings.detail: Model (Sameni, Clifford, Jutten, Shamsollahi 2007, EURASIP JASP 2007:043407): a single rotating and translating dipole, linked to body-surface potentials by a linear model. Differential form (PhysioNet simPAF_DipoleGenerator): dtheta/dt = omega; dx/dt = -sum_i (alpha_i^x*omega/(b_i^x)^2)*dtheta_i*exp(-dtheta_i^2/(2*(b_i^x)^2)), where dtheta_i = wrap(theta - theta_i) to (-pi, pi]. Same for y and z. Integrated form: x(theta) = sum_i alpha_i^x*exp(-dtheta_i^2/(2*b_i^2)). R peak at theta = 0. Normal parameters from FECGSYN load_gparam 'normal' case 1 ('old1'). That code cites Behar 2014 and PTB healthy controls, not the Sameni table, so the match to Sameni 2007 is unverified. X: theta = [-1.09,-0.83,-0.19,-0.07,0,0.06,0.22,1.2,1.42,1.68]; alpha = [0.03,0.08,-0.13,0.85,1.11,0.75,0.06,0.1,0.17,0.39]; b = [0.0906,0.1057,0.0453,0.0378,0.0332,0.0302,0.0378,0.6040,0.3020,0.1812]. Y: theta = [-1.1,-0.9,-0.76,-0.11,-0.01,0.065,0.8,1.58]; alpha = [0.035,0.015,-0.019,0.32,0.51,-0.32,0.04,0.08]; b = [0.07,0.07,0.04,0.055,0.037,0.0604,0.45,0.3]. Z: theta = [-1.1,-0.93,-0.7,-0.4,-0.15,0.095,1.05,1.25,1.55]; alpha = [-0.03,-0.14,-0.035,0.045,-0.4,0.46,-0.12,-0.2,-0.35]; b = [0.03,0.12,0.04,0.4,0.045,0.05,0.8,0.4,0.2]. Units appear to be mV; that is inferred, not stated. Case 2 and an 'ectopic' set (11 Gaussians per axis) are also in load_gparam. At 60 bpm, 1 rad = 159 ms, so the QRS Gaussians span about -0.28 to +0.30 rad, roughly 90 ms (derived).

findings.topic: 7a. Lead mapping: 12-lead formulas, Dower lead vectors, and a projection test
findings.detail: Lead formulas (bem.fi ch.15): I = PhiL - PhiR; II = PhiF - PhiR; III = PhiF - PhiL; WCT = (PhiR + PhiL + PhiF)/3; aVR = PhiR - (PhiL + PhiF)/2; aVL = PhiL - (PhiR + PhiF)/2; aVF = PhiF - (PhiR + PhiL)/2; Vi = PhiVi - WCT. Over 90% of the heart's electrical activity is explained by a dipole. Inverse Dower matrix as printed in Guillem CinC 2006 (rows X, Y, Z; columns V1-V6, I, II): X = [-0.172,-0.073,0.122,0.231,0.239,0.193,0.156,-0.009]; Y = [0.057,-0.019,-0.106,-0.022,0.040,0.048,-0.227,0.886]; Z = [-0.228,-0.310,-0.245,-0.063,0.054,0.108,0.021,0.102]. Forward Dower, obtained as the pseudoinverse of the Edenbrandt-Pahlm inverse (rows [X,Y,Z]): V1 [-0.515,0.157,-0.917]; V2 [0.044,0.164,-1.387]; V3 [0.882,0.098,-1.277]; V4 [1.213,0.127,-0.601]; V5 [1.125,0.127,-0.086]; V6 [0.831,0.076,0.230]; I [0.632,-0.235,0.059]; II [0.235,1.066,-0.132]. The pseudoinverse matched these to within 0.004. On PTB data the Dower QRS loop error is 121 µV RMS vs 85 µV for a least-squares matrix. Correlation for Z (0.84) is weaker than for X (0.93). My projection test (FECGSYN normal through forward Dower) gave R/S in mV of: I 0.80/-0.12, II 0.80/-0.25, III 0.40/-0.75, aVR 0.05/-0.77, aVL 0.72/-0.24, aVF 0.45/-0.44, V1 0.42/-0.84, V2 0.60/-0.61, V3 1.22/-0.37, V4 1.70/-0.12, V5 1.60/-0.10, V6 1.19/-0.15. T peaks: I 0.32, II 0.30, aVR -0.31, V1 0.33, V2 0.88, V3 1.25, V4 1.05, V6 0.38. Frontal QRS axis by area +17 deg; T axis +36 deg; transition V2-V3; peak spatial QRS 1.44 mV and T 0.82 mV; spatial QRS-T angle 48 deg. So this one subject's set is leftward of the +60 deg target and has large anterior T waves.

Transition (R/S > 1) normally at V3 or V4; V2 counts as early and V5 as delayed but still normal. Upper normal QRS duration under 120 ms, often under 110 ms. T upright in V2-V6 and inverted in aVR. Poor R progression: R in V3 of 3 mm or less. P: under 120 ms, under 0.25 mV in limb leads, axis 0 to +75. SVG 79-107 mV·ms (sex-dependent). Population normal limits (2nd-98th percentile by age) are in Rijnbeek 2014 (13,354 healthy people aged 16-90, J Electrocardiol 47:914) at normalecg.org. PTB Diagnostic DB (PhysioNet) has the 12 standard leads plus Frank vx, vy, vz recorded together at 1 kHz from 294 subjects, which is a good target for fitting H(t).

Boonstra 2022: a 'normal' activation from 6 sites with uniform 0.85 m/s produced clinically abnormal ECG patterns: V1 RS, prominent S in V6, QS in aVR, QR in aVL. Matching one patient needed 8 foci tuned at 1 m/s (QRS 100 ms). The more realistic route is to include the His-Purkinje effect (Boonstra, Ann Biomed Eng 2022). The diseased-patch study shows QRS changes in V1 depend on patch location. Slowing alone to 0.25 m/s barely changes body-surface potentials, while patchy activation (0-90 ms jitter) causes fragmentation. Szathmary: the dipole approximation is weakest in mid-QRS (up to 28.5% deviation, mainly in the anterior-posterior and inferior-superior components). Precordial-lead shape is therefore the hardest part, and the place where an infinite-medium single dipole is least reliable.

recommendations: Source model: use EDL faces taken directly from the Three.js ventricular mesh, a few hundred to a few thousand triangles, each tagged with one of the 12-20 regions. Per time step: s_p(t) = [1/(1+exp(-(t-delta_p)/tau_u))] * [1 - a*(t-delta_p)/200 ms] * [1/(1+exp((t-rho_p)/tau_r))]; m_p = -tau*A_p*n_p*s_p; H = sum of m_p, with tau = 8 mA/m. Check closure (|sum A_p*n_p| under 1% of sum A_p) and add a basal cap if needed. Starting values: a = 0.05-0.2; tau_u about 1-2 ms and tau_r about 10-20 ms (both unsourced, so tune them).

Activation times per face, not per region: run a Dijkstra/fastest-route pass on the mesh graph. Seed it at Purkinje exit sites given by the conduction graph: three LV endocardial sites at 0-5 ms (anterior paraseptal, posterior paraseptal, mid-left septum) and the RV anterior papillary-muscle base at 5-10 ms. Use 0.85 m/s along the surface and about 0.34 m/s across the wall; a fast endocardial (Purkinje) layer can use 2-4 m/s. Targets: RV epicardial breakthrough under 25 ms, all breakthroughs by 40 ms, last activation at the basal posterolateral LV / RV outflow tract at about 80-95 ms. This avoids the stair-step QRS you get when a whole region switches at once.

APD map tied to anatomy, not to activation: APD_p = 235 ms + G_ab*(normalized apex-to-base coordinate) + G_tm*(1 for endocardium, 0 for epicardium) + G_lr*(1 if LV). Defaults: G_ab of +40 to +65 ms (apex repolarizes first); G_tm of +20 to +30 ms; G_lr small (0 to ±10 ms) because the sources disagree. rho_p = delta_p + APD_p. Optionally add the electrotonic APD shortening for later activation (slope up to -1.44 ms/ms in the epicardium, Cowan 1988). Keep it near 0 so that BBB, PVC and pacing keep a discordant T. Unit tests: (1) normal T concordant in I, II, V3-V6; (2) LBBB/RBBB/RV pacing reached only by moving seeds gives discordant ST-T with G almost unchanged; (3) G magnitude about 80-110 mV·ms once scaled to Frank mV.

Leads, primary path: map app coordinates to Frank (X = patient left, Y = feet, Z = back; confirm the signs). Scale H by k (mV per A·m) so the peak spatial QRS is 1.4-1.8 mV. Compute V1-V6, I and II with the forward Dower rows, then III = II - I, aVR = -(I+II)/2, aVL = I - II/2, aVF = II - I/2. Every lead is then a fixed projection of the same H(t).

Leads, educational/electrode-moving path: phi_e = Gt/(4*pi*sigma) * sum_p m_p·(r_e - x_p)/|r_e - x_p|^3 with sigma = 0.2 S/m, summed over faces rather than one centroid dipole, which helps V1-V3. Place the RA/LA/LL virtual electrodes at the shoulders and left groin, then form WCT and the 12 leads. Pick Gt (about 2-3, unsourced) or a per-lead gain so lead II and V4 match the Dower path for the normal beat. Show the Dower path as the 'clinical' trace.

Calibration loop (normal): tune in this order. (i) Septal initial vector (LV septum 5-10 ms before RV) for q in I, aVL, V5-V6 and r in V1. (ii) Frontal axis, toward +30 to +60 deg, via the relative timing of anterior vs posterior fascicle seeds and the heart's long-axis orientation. (iii) Transition at V3-V4, via late posterobasal LV and RV outflow activation (posterior/superior terminal forces deepen S in V1-V2). (iv) QRS 80-100 ms. (v) T amplitude via G_ab and the plateau slope 'a'. Use FECGSYN normal or PTB Frank leads as the target VCG and score the fit by loop correlation per axis.

Disease hooks, all on the same H(t): old MI = set s = 0 on a region's faces and add rim faces carrying the region's negative area vector, activated with the neighbouring wall. This gives Q waves and keeps ST flat; the Selvester rule of thumb is about 3% of LV per point. Acute STEMI = plateau eps of about 0.2-0.4 on that region's epicardial and endocardial faces, plus a resting offset r of about 0.1-0.2 for TQ depression. Subendocardial ischemia = same edit on endocardial faces only, giving ST depression. Scale so the ST deviation is 0.1-0.5 mV. Hyperacute T = locally shorter APD. BBB = remove the RBB or LBB seeds and let the wave cross the septum slowly (0.85 m/s or slower).

Atria: thin walls make the EDL endocardial/epicardial cancellation numerically fragile. Use a wavefront-dipole sum instead: H_A(t) = sum_j g_j*B_j(t)*d_j, where d_j is the local direction of travel along conduction-graph edges (SA node to RA, Bachmann's bundle to LA, ending at the LA appendage), B_j is a smooth bump over the region's activation window, and atrial velocity is 0.8-1.0 m/s. Calibrate the total to P of about 0.1-0.2 mV in II, under 120 ms, axis about +45 to +60. Ta wave = negative, low-pass-smeared copy of the P vector over about 300 ms, scaled to about -25 µV in II. P-mitrale: delay the LA by 20-40 ms and enlarge its posterior-leftward component. P-pulmonale: enlarge the RA inferior component so P in II exceeds 0.25 mV.

Flutter: H_F(t) = A*[u*cos(phi) + v*sin(phi)], one rotation per 170-250 ms (240-350/min), with uneven angular speed (slow through the isthmus) to make the sawtooth. Choose u and v so II goes trough, V1 peak, II peak, V1 trough (counterclockwise), with negative waves in II/III/aVF and positive in V1. AF: sum 3-6 wavelets with random directions, 4-9 Hz Stridh-style sawtooth signals (M = 3, a0 of about 0.06 mV, frequency and amplitude random walks), with directions drifting slowly so the loops never repeat; target about 50 µV in V1.

Fallback if the morphology cannot be tuned: keep the region model but fit it. Take each region's unit time course h_r(t) from the EDL (or a Gaussian bump along the region normal at its activation time) and solve non-negative least squares for weights w_r so that sum w_r*h_r(t) matches a target VCG (FECGSYN normal or a PTB Frank recording). Disease edits (zeroing a region, changing timing, injury eps) still act on the fitted sources, so every lead stays a projection of one source. Last resort: drive H(t) straight from the Sameni Gaussian VCG through Dower, with region-highlight animation synced to the phase.
unsourced: Frank axis signs (X+ = patient left, Y+ = feet, Z+ = back) are inferred from the inverse Dower signs and the FECGSYN loop polarities; I did not read them in a source. Confirm before mapping to Three.js Y-up coordinates, because a flipped axis would invert precordial or inferior leads.

The forward Dower coefficients are the pseudoinverse of an inverse-Dower matrix I typed from memory (Edenbrandt & Pahlm 1988). That matrix agrees with Guillem CinC 2006's printed one to about ±0.002, and the forward values match commonly cited Dower 1980 values; the original Dower table itself was not retrieved.

The derivation H = -tau*sum(A_p*n_p*s_p) (gradient theorem on J_i = -sigma*grad(Vm)), its sign, and the closure and ventricular-gradient consequences are my own. Check them with a unit test where the endocardium activates first and H must point endocardium to epicardium.
The FECGSYN normal case 1 may or may not equal Table 1 of Sameni 2007, and the mV unit is inferred. The 12-lead projection numbers (+17 deg axis, 48 deg QRS-T angle, etc.) are my own computation.

TMP time constants (upstroke 1-2 ms, repolarization sigmoid 10-20 ms), wall thicknesses (LV about 10 mm, RV 3-5 mm) and the torso boundary gain of about 2-3 for infinite-medium potentials come from general knowledge.
Placing limb electrodes virtually at the shoulders and groin (limbs act as linear conductors) is general electrophysiology knowledge; I did not verify it in a source.

Details of Miller & Geselowitz 1978 (often described as about 23 regional dipoles driven by regional action potentials in an inhomogeneous torso), Selvester's original multi-dipole model, and Holt/Barnard or Aoki/Okamoto models could not be retrieved. No region lists or timing tables are given for them.
The Selvester lead-to-segment mapping (V1-V2 septal, V3-V4 anterior, I/aVL/V5-V6 lateral, II/aVF inferior, tall R in V1-V2 = posterior) and the per-lead point criteria are from general knowledge.

Mapping ischemia to EDL parameters (plateau reduction eps of 0.2-0.4, rest offset r of 0.1-0.2) is my own conversion from the 30 mV bidomain difference. Typical clinical STEMI magnitudes of 1-5 mm are general knowledge.
The exact Stridh & Sörnmo 2001 sawtooth formula (harmonic weights 2/(i*pi), modulation frequencies) was recalled from memory. The parameters given come from Malik 2017's generalized version.

The flutter rotation-plane orientation, flutter amplitude, P-mitrale interpeak notch over 40 ms, the AF multi-wavelet direction model, and the suggested regions (AHA 17-segment LV plus 3-5 RV regions) are unsourced design choices.

Ta amplitudes of about -25 µV in II come from a search snippet of a Hull repository paper whose authors I could not confirm. The Holmqvist 2009 Frank-lead values (-6.9 µV in Y) were taken from an automated summary that also mislabelled the Ta/P amplitude ratio.
